title: Spaced repetition in care training starts with a question they cannot guess. A fresh one shows understanding.
meta_title: Spaced Repetition for Care Staff Training | CareStreamAI
meta_description: Some carers guess their way through a quiz. A short lesson then a fresh question shows real understanding, and you can set the topic again later.
lede: Some staff pass the quiz by guessing, and nobody can tell. The idea behind spaced repetition is simple: come back to a topic over time so it sticks. With training built from your own policies, a wrong answer leads to a short lesson and a fresh question, so a lucky guess does not close the gap.

intro.heading: She passed. Did she know it, or did she get lucky?
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A carer finishes the fire safety module on her phone between visits to rooms. The score looks fine, so nobody looks twice. In the staff room she admits she was guessing answers on half of it, and picked the one that sounded most sensible. She is not careless. She is tired, the wording was new, and the next call bell was ringing. The manager only sees a pass. Weeks later a fire alarm goes off on a night shift, and the question that was guessed is the one that matters. Here is how that plays out.

trail.text: The day team is asked to complete the fire safety module on their phones.
One carer finishes it in ten minutes and gets a pass.
The manager sees a completed module and a green tick.
Three answers were picked because they sounded right, not because she knew.
A lucky guess and real understanding look the same on a pass mark.
Nobody revisits the topic, so the little she knew fades.
A tick that does not say what she could do in a fire.
“What would you do if the alarm sounded?” A tick is not an answer.

trail_close: A pass mark can hide guessing. The fix is not a harder quiz. It is a way to check again, on the same point, with a question she has not seen.

why.heading: A score tells you she answered, not that she understood
why.sub: Guessing is human. The aim is to make it visible and then give it a second chance.

cards.title: Multiple choice rewards a good guess
cards.body: With three or four options, a plausible answer is often right by chance. A carer who is rushed or unsure of the wording can pass without knowing the point.

cards.title: Asking the same question twice proves little
cards.body: If someone sees the identical question again, they may remember the answer from last time, not the reason behind it. A new question on the same point tests more.

cards.title: One pass does not last
cards.body: Knowledge fades if it is never used. Without a reason to come back to a topic, the little that was learned slips away before it is needed.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: Half my team probably guess some answers. How would I even know?
items.a: A score alone will not show it. What shows it is a wrong answer followed by a fresh question. If a carer gets one wrong, it goes into their Follow-up tab, and the lesson then asks a different question on the same point. The Knowledge gaps view shows which questions are missed most often across the team.

items.q: What happens when someone gets a question wrong?
items.a: It goes straight into their Follow-up tab in the Staff Hub, and they get an email, at most once a day and in English. They choose Learn & retry, a short lesson with a fresh question, or Just retry, the same question again. They can retry as often as they need.

items.q: Is the new question really different, or the same one reworded?
items.a: After the short lesson, Learn & retry asks one fresh multiple choice question on that point. It is not the original question, so a lucky guess the first time does not close the gap. Just retry does repeat the same question, so it suits a carer who only needs another look.

items.q: Does CareStream do spaced repetition automatically?
items.a: No. It does not schedule repeat questions on its own. What it does is let you allocate a module again whenever you choose, for example a few weeks after the first round. That gives you the same spacing effect, but you decide when, and you can add a due date.

items.q: Will it tell me every time someone gets one wrong?
items.a: No. Nothing alerts you on each wrong answer. You see the picture in Analytics under Knowledge gaps, and in a Monday digest email. The carer sees their own Follow-up tab straight away.

items.q: Is the lesson about fire safety in general or about our home?
items.a: Where your own policies cover the topic, the lesson draws on them, so it reflects what your home does. Where they do not, it falls back on general good practice. You can edit and preview the module before anyone sees it, and the carer's lesson is generated when they tap Learn & retry.

items.q: Can a carer who reads English as a second language use this?
items.a: Yes, on the paid plans, where training can be shown in the language they think in. The reminder email to the carer is English only, so tell the team to look at the Follow-up tab in the hub. Translation is machine translation and not on the free plan.

items.q: Can I try it before I commit?
items.a: Yes. There is a 14 day free trial on the paid plans, and you can create a free account to look around. The adhoc training screen is on the paid plans, so use the trial to build one fire safety module and allocate it to a few staff.

limits.heading: A way to check and revisit, not proof of understanding

cards.title: It does not stop guessing answers
cards.body: A carer can still guess on any question. What changes is that a wrong guess opens a lesson and a fresh question, which makes guessing answers less likely to go unnoticed.

cards.title: It does not repeat questions on a timetable
cards.body: There is no automatic schedule of repeat questions. If you want to revisit a topic, you allocate the module again. Adhoc training and translation are on the paid plans only.

cards.title: It does not tell you each time someone slips
cards.body: Nothing alerts you on each wrong answer. You see patterns in Knowledge gaps and the Monday digest. Hands on skills, like using an evacuation sledge, still need a person to show and watch them.

faqs.heading: Guessing, quizzes and revisiting a topic, answered

items.q: What is spaced repetition in care training?
items.a: It means coming back to a topic at intervals instead of covering it once. In a care home that could be a short fire safety check a few weeks after the main session. CareStream does not schedule it for you, but you can allocate a module again in the Training screen whenever you choose.

items.q: What is retrieval practice, and does it help?
items.a: Retrieval practice means recalling something from memory, such as answering a question, rather than just reading it again. Recalling an answer tends to help learning, which is why a fresh question after a lesson is useful. It is a helpful idea, not a promise about results.

items.q: How do I stop staff guessing answers on a training quiz?
items.a: You cannot stop it completely, but you can make it visible and less rewarding. A wrong answer leads to a lesson and a fresh question, and the Knowledge gaps view shows the questions missed most. Explaining to staff that a wrong answer is information, not blame, helps too.

items.q: What makes a good knowledge check?
items.a: Keep it short, tie each question to one point, and ask about what the person would do. Avoid trick wording. Preview the questions first so you know they match your home's own procedure, which you can do before allocating.

items.q: How is a check for understanding different from a training quiz?
items.a: A training quiz often ends with a score. A check for understanding asks whether the person can apply the point, and does something when they cannot. In CareStream a wrong answer opens a lesson and a fresh question, so the check carries on until they have it.

items.q: Does it work for other topics, not just fire safety?
items.a: Yes. Pick any topic module, such as safeguarding or infection control. Fire safety is only the example here.

items.q: Does the law say fire safety training must be repeated?
items.a: The Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005, article 21, says employee training must be repeated periodically where appropriate. It does not set a fixed interval, so you decide what is appropriate for your home.

items.q: What does CQC say about staff training?
items.a: Regulation 18 says staff must receive the support, training, professional development, supervision and appraisal they need to do their jobs. Questions, lessons and results help you show that staff understand, not only attended. See also CQC and compliance.

guide.heading: A practical way to tell a guess from understanding
guide.lede: You do not need a new system. You need a short check, a lesson when it goes wrong, and a habit of coming back to the topic.

paragraphs: If the same question comes back, a carer may recall the shape of the right answer without knowing why it is right. A fresh question on the same point asks them to use the idea. That is why Learn & retry follows a short lesson with a new question.
Keep your own tone kind. Tell the team that a wrong answer is how the system finds a gap, and that guessing is common when training is squeezed into a busy shift.

sections.h3: Four habits that fit a busy service
checklist: Allocate a short module on the topic, built from your policies, and preview it first.
Remind staff to open the Follow-up tab in the hub when they have a wrong answer.
Each month, look at the most missed questions and weakest topics in Knowledge gaps.
After a few weeks, allocate the module again if the topic matters, such as fire safety.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the questions, the lessons and the results together. They show that you checked understanding, not only completion.
